en.q: What is the single most effective way to prevent healthcare-associated infections?
o: Wearing gloves for every patient contact
Performing hand hygiene at the right moments
Keeping the patient in a private room
en.e: Hand hygiene (WHO "5 moments") is the most effective measure. Gloves never replace hand hygiene.

en.q: A nurse's hands are visibly soiled with body fluids. The nurse should:
o: Wash hands with soap and water
Wipe hands with a dry paper towel
en.e: Alcohol rubs do not remove visible dirt or organic material. Wash with soap and water when hands are visibly soiled.

en.q: A patient has Clostridioides difficile diarrhea. Which measures are correct?
o: Contact precautions and hand washing with soap and water
Airborne precautions and alcohol hand rub only
en.e: C. difficile spores are not reliably killed by alcohol. Use contact precautions, gloves and gown, and wash with soap and water.

en.q: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis requires:
o: A surgical mask for staff and a regular room
Airborne precautions with an N95 (or higher) respirator and a negative-pressure room
No special precautions until culture results
en.e: TB spreads by airborne droplet nuclei. Place the patient in an airborne infection isolation room and wear a fit-tested respirator.

en.q: Which infection requires droplet precautions?
en.e: Influenza, pertussis and meningococcal disease need droplet precautions. Measles and varicella need airborne precautions.

en.q: What is the recommended order for putting on (donning) PPE?
o: Gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, gloves
en.e: Gloves go on last so they cover the gown cuffs. When removing PPE, gloves (the most contaminated) usually come off first.

en.q: Before giving a medication, the nurse must identify the patient using:
o: At least two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth
The name on the door sign
en.e: Two patient identifiers are an international patient safety goal. Room numbers are never used as identifiers.

en.q: Which action best reduces the risk of falls for an older patient at night?
o: Keeping the bed in the lowest position with the call bell within reach
en.e: Low bed, call bell, non-slip footwear, night light and regular rounding reduce falls. Four raised rails can increase injury.

en.q: A patient in physical restraints should have restraints released for skin care and range of motion at least every:
en.e: Monitor frequently, and release restraints at least every 2 hours (or per policy) to check skin, circulation and offer fluids and toileting.

en.q: A pressure injury with partial-thickness skin loss and exposed pink dermis is classified as:
en.e: Stage 1 is intact skin with non-blanchable redness. Stage 3 involves full-thickness loss into fat; stage 4 exposes muscle, tendon or bone.

en.q: Which nursing action best prevents pressure injuries in an immobile patient?
o: Repositioning at least every 2 hours and using a pressure-redistributing surface
Keeping the head of the bed at 90 degrees all day
en.e: Regular repositioning, skin assessment, nutrition and moisture control prevent pressure injuries. Donut cushions and massage are not recommended.

en.q: When caring for several patients, which need is the nurse's first priority?
en.e: Use the ABC priority framework: airway, breathing, circulation, then other needs.

en.q: The normal resting respiratory rate for an adult is:
en.e: Adults normally breathe 12–20 times a minute. Report persistent rates outside this range in context.

en.q: A fire starts in a patient's room. Following RACE, the nurse's first action is to:
o: Contain the fire by closing doors
en.e: RACE = Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish/Evacuate. To use an extinguisher, remember PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep.

en.q: Which task can a registered nurse delegate to an unlicensed assistant?
o: Teaching a patient to self-inject insulin
Measuring vital signs of a stable patient
Evaluating a patient's response to a new medication
en.e: Assessment, teaching and evaluation stay with the RN. Routine tasks for stable patients may be delegated.

en.q: In obtaining informed consent for surgery, the nurse's role is usually to:
o: Explain the risks and benefits of the procedure
Witness the patient's signature and confirm the patient understands
Decide whether the patient needs surgery
Sign the form on behalf of the patient
en.e: The surgeon explains the procedure, risks and alternatives. The nurse witnesses and reports if the patient seems uninformed.

en.q: In the SBAR communication tool, "A" stands for:
en.e: SBAR = Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. It structures handover and calls to physicians.

en.q: After giving an injection, the nurse should:
o: Recap the needle using both hands
Discard the uncapped needle immediately in a puncture-resistant sharps container
Place the needle in the regular trash
en.e: Never recap used needles with two hands. Immediate disposal prevents needlestick injuries.

en.q: The normal oxygen saturation (SpO2) range for a healthy adult is about:
en.e: Targets may be lower for some patients, such as those with chronic CO2 retention (often 88–92%).

en.q: A patient refuses a prescribed medication. The nurse should first:
o: Give it anyway because it was prescribed
Explore the reason for refusal, document it and inform the prescriber
Ask a family member to give it
en.e: Competent adults have the right to refuse treatment. Explore concerns, educate, document and notify.

en.q: A diabetic patient is shaky, sweaty and confused, with a blood glucose of 50 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L). The patient is awake and can swallow. The nurse should first:
o: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, then recheck glucose in 15 minutes
en.e: This is the "rule of 15." If the patient cannot swallow, give IV dextrose or glucagon per protocol.

en.q: Which finding is typical of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?
o: Deep, rapid (Kussmaul) respirations and fruity breath odor
en.e: DKA causes hyperglycemia, ketosis and metabolic acidosis. Treatment includes IV fluids, insulin infusion and potassium monitoring.

en.q: Which insulin can be given intravenously?
en.e: Regular (short-acting) insulin is the type used in IV insulin infusions.

en.q: Which finding is most consistent with left-sided heart failure?
o: Crackles in the lungs and dyspnea
en.e: Left-sided failure backs fluid into the lungs. Right-sided failure causes systemic congestion such as edema, JVD and hepatomegaly.

en.q: Which blood test is most specific for myocardial injury?
en.e: Cardiac troponins rise within hours of myocardial injury and are the preferred biomarker.

en.q: A patient with an acute ischemic stroke may receive IV thrombolysis (alteplase) if:
o: Symptoms started more than 24 hours ago
A CT scan rules out hemorrhage and treatment can start within about 4.5 hours of symptom onset
The patient has a recent major surgery
Blood pressure is 220/130 mmHg and untreated
en.e: Time is brain. Hemorrhage must be excluded first, and eligibility criteria and blood pressure limits must be met.

en.q: For a patient with COPD and chronic CO2 retention, oxygen is usually titrated to a target SpO2 of:
en.e: Controlled oxygen avoids worsening hypercapnia while preventing hypoxemia.

en.q: In a chest drainage system, continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber usually indicates:
o: An air leak in the system or from the patient
Re-expansion of the lung is complete
en.e: Gentle tidaling is normal. Continuous bubbling suggests an air leak; check connections from the patient to the unit.

en.q: After a thyroidectomy, the patient reports tingling around the mouth and fingers. The nurse should suspect:
en.e: Check for Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs and have IV calcium gluconate available.

en.q: Which ECG change is classic for hyperkalemia?
en.e: Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves and can progress to wide QRS and dangerous arrhythmias. U waves suggest hypokalemia.

en.q: The normal serum potassium range for an adult is approximately:
en.e: Normal potassium is about 3.5–5.0 mmol/L. (135–145 mmol/L is the normal sodium range.)

en.q: Which intervention best helps prevent atelectasis after abdominal surgery?
o: Keeping the patient flat in bed
Incentive spirometry, deep breathing and early ambulation
en.e: Adequate pain control allows effective deep breathing and coughing.

en.q: Which finding most suggests deep vein thrombosis?
o: Unilateral calf swelling, warmth and pain
en.e: Report suspected DVT. Do not massage the leg. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by ultrasound.

en.q: A post-operative patient suddenly develops chest pain, shortness of breath and tachycardia. The nurse should suspect:
en.e: Raise the head of the bed, give oxygen, stay with the patient and notify the provider urgently.

en.q: Lactulose is given to a patient with cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy mainly to:
o: Reduce ammonia absorption from the bowel
en.e: Lactulose traps ammonia in the colon and causes 2–3 soft stools a day.

en.q: The most common causes of peptic ulcer disease are:
o: Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID use
en.e: Treatment often includes eradication therapy for H. pylori and stopping NSAIDs.

en.q: For a patient with an arteriovenous fistula for hemodialysis, the nurse should:
o: Take blood pressure on the fistula arm
Avoid BP and venipuncture on that arm and check for a thrill and bruit
Apply a tight bandage over the fistula
en.e: A palpable thrill and audible bruit show the fistula is patent.

en.q: Which precaution is appropriate for a patient with severe neutropenia?
o: Allowing fresh flowers in the room
Strict hand hygiene and avoiding visitors who are ill
en.e: Neutropenic patients are at high risk of infection. Avoid rectal procedures and sources of pathogens.

en.q: A Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 or less usually indicates:
o: Severe brain injury, with a need to protect the airway
en.e: GCS ranges from 3 to 15. "Eight, intubate" is a common teaching phrase.

en.q: Which is an early sign of increasing intracranial pressure?
o: A change in level of consciousness
en.e: Changes in LOC (restlessness, confusion) are the earliest signs. Cushing's triad and fixed pupils are late signs.

en.q: Before giving digoxin to an adult, the nurse should:
o: Check the radial pulse for 15 seconds
Check the apical pulse for one full minute and withhold if below 60 (or per order)
Give it with potassium supplements always
en.e: Also monitor potassium levels, because hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity.

en.q: Which symptoms suggest digoxin toxicity?
o: Nausea, vomiting and visual disturbances such as yellow-green halos
en.e: Bradycardia and dysrhythmias may also occur. Check serum digoxin and potassium levels.

en.q: Warfarin therapy is monitored using:
en.e: Vitamin K is the antidote. Teach consistent intake of vitamin K–rich foods.

en.q: The antidote for heparin overdose is:
en.e: Unfractionated heparin is monitored with aPTT (or anti-Xa levels).

en.q: A patient taking furosemide should be monitored especially for:
en.e: Loop diuretics cause loss of potassium. Monitor electrolytes, BP, weight and intake and output.

en.q: A patient taking spironolactone should be taught to avoid:
o: Potassium supplements and salt substitutes that contain potassium
en.e: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and can cause hyperkalemia.

en.q: A common side effect of ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril is:
en.e: Angioedema is a rare but serious reaction. Hyperkalemia can also occur.

en.q: Beta blockers such as metoprolol should be used with caution in patients with:
en.e: Beta blockers slow the heart and non-selective ones can cause bronchospasm. Check pulse and BP before giving.

en.q: The antidote for opioid overdose is:
en.e: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, so continue to monitor respirations.

en.q: The antidote for benzodiazepine overdose is:
en.e: Use flumazenil cautiously; it can trigger seizures in long-term benzodiazepine users.

en.q: The antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) overdose is:
en.e: Acetylcysteine protects the liver and works best when started early.

en.q: A patient receiving IV magnesium sulfate for preeclampsia has a respiratory rate of 10 and absent reflexes. The nurse should stop the infusion and prepare:
en.e: These are signs of magnesium toxicity. Calcium gluconate is the antidote.

en.q: Which statement about IV potassium chloride is correct?
o: It may be given by IV push in emergencies
It must be diluted and given by infusion, never by IV push
It should be given faster when urine output is low
It does not require cardiac monitoring at any rate
en.e: Undiluted or IV push potassium can cause fatal arrhythmias. Confirm adequate urine output.

en.q: The order is amoxicillin 500 mg orally. The suspension contains 250 mg per 5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give?
1,000 mL of normal saline is to be infused over 8 hours. What is the hourly rate?
An infusion is to run at 100 mL/h using a set with a drop factor of 20 drops/mL. How many drops per minute?
en.e: 100 mL × 20 drops ÷ 60 minutes = 33.3, about 33 drops/min.

en.q: A child weighing 20 kg is prescribed 15 mg/kg of a drug. What is the dose?
en.e: 15 mg × 20 kg = 300 mg. Always check that the dose is within the safe range.

en.q: Heparin 25,000 units in 500 mL is ordered at 1,000 units per hour. What is the pump rate?
Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin can cause:
en.e: Monitor kidney function, hearing and peak and trough drug levels.

en.q: Flushing and a red rash on the face and neck during a vancomycin infusion usually means:
o: The infusion is too fast (vancomycin infusion reaction)
en.e: Slow the infusion. Vancomycin is usually given over at least 60 minutes.

en.q: The normal fetal heart rate baseline is:
en.e: Persistent rates outside this range need evaluation.

en.q: Late decelerations on the fetal monitor indicate:
en.e: Turn the mother to her side, stop oxytocin, give IV fluids and oxygen per protocol, and notify the provider.

en.q: Variable decelerations are most often caused by:
en.e: Repositioning the mother is usually the first action.

en.q: Early decelerations that mirror contractions are caused by:
o: Fetal head compression and are usually benign
en.e: Early decelerations are common during descent and need no intervention.

en.q: A postpartum woman has heavy bleeding and a soft, boggy uterus. The nurse's first action is to:
en.e: Uterine atony is the leading cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Fundal massage and uterotonic drugs help the uterus contract.

en.q: About 24 hours after birth, the fundus is normally found:
o: At the level of the xiphoid process
At or about 1 cm below the umbilicus
en.e: The fundus then descends about 1 cm per day.

en.q: Preeclampsia is defined as new hypertension after 20 weeks of gestation with:
o: Proteinuria or signs of organ dysfunction
en.e: Warning signs include headache, visual changes and epigastric pain.

en.q: An Rh-negative mother who gives birth to an Rh-positive baby should receive anti-D immunoglobulin:
o: Only if the baby is jaundiced
en.e: It is also commonly given at about 28 weeks of gestation to prevent sensitization.

en.q: The APGAR score is assessed at:
en.e: It assesses heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability and color.

en.q: Newborns receive an IM injection of vitamin K to:
en.e: Newborns have low vitamin K levels and a sterile gut at birth.

en.q: Jaundice that appears within the first 24 hours of life is:
en.e: Physiologic jaundice usually appears after 24 hours.

en.q: A healthy infant usually doubles birth weight by about:
en.e: Birth weight usually triples by about 12 months.

en.q: A child with suspected epiglottitis is drooling and sitting in the tripod position. The nurse should:
o: Inspect the throat with a tongue depressor
Avoid examining the throat and prepare for emergency airway management
en.e: Examining the throat can cause complete airway obstruction.

en.q: Which sign suggests dehydration in an infant?
o: A sunken fontanelle and fewer wet diapers
en.e: Other signs include dry mouth, no tears and lethargy.

en.q: Children with cystic fibrosis usually take pancreatic enzyme supplements:
en.e: Enzymes help digest fats and proteins. Diets are usually high-calorie.

en.q: The MMR vaccine is:
o: A live attenuated vaccine, usually first given at 12–15 months
An inactivated vaccine given at birth
en.e: Live vaccines are generally avoided in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency.

en.q: Lochia rubra (bright red discharge) normally lasts about:
en.e: It is followed by lochia serosa (pinkish-brown) and then lochia alba (whitish).

en.q: Which statement about breastfeeding is correct?
o: Newborns should be fed only every 6 hours
Feeding on demand, about 8–12 times in 24 hours, is recommended
Formula must be given after each breastfeed
Breastfeeding should stop if the mother has sore nipples
en.e: Exclusive breastfeeding for about the first six months is recommended by WHO.

en.q: When calculating a pediatric medication dose, the nurse should always:
o: Verify the dose against the child's weight (mg/kg) and the safe range
en.e: Weight-based checks are essential to prevent pediatric dosing errors.

en.q: A child with croup typically presents with:
o: A productive cough and high fever
A barking, seal-like cough and inspiratory stridor
en.e: Cool mist, steroids and nebulized epinephrine are common treatments. Watch for respiratory distress.

en.q: For an adult in cardiac arrest, chest compressions should be given at a rate of:
en.e: Push at least 5 cm (2 inches) deep, allow full recoil and minimize interruptions.

en.q: For adult CPR with one rescuer, the compression-to-ventilation ratio is:
en.e: 30:2 is used for adults. It changes once an advanced airway is placed.

en.q: The first-line drug for anaphylaxis is:
en.e: Give IM epinephrine (often into the anterolateral thigh) promptly, then support airway, breathing and circulation.

en.q: In mass-casualty triage, a patient who can walk to the treatment area is usually tagged:
en.e: "Walking wounded" are triaged as minor.

en.q: Using the rule of nines, an adult with burns to the entire right arm has burns to about what percentage of body surface area?
en.e: Each arm is 9%; each leg 18%; front and back of the trunk 18% each; head 9%; perineum 1%.

en.q: Using the Parkland formula, half of the 24-hour fluid requirement is given:
o: In the first 8 hours after the burn
en.e: Parkland: 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA. The time counts from the burn, not from arrival.

en.q: Which findings suggest hypovolemic shock?
o: Bradycardia, warm dry skin and high urine output
Tachycardia, hypotension, cool clammy skin and low urine output
en.e: Restore volume and find the cause of fluid or blood loss.

en.q: For a patient with suspected sepsis, broad-spectrum antibiotics should be started:
o: As soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour, after blood cultures are taken
Only if the patient has a fever
en.e: Early antibiotics and fluid resuscitation improve survival.

en.q: Cushing's triad, a late sign of increased intracranial pressure, consists of:
o: Hypertension with widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations
en.e: Cushing's triad suggests impending brain herniation and is a medical emergency.

en.q: An ABG shows pH 7.30, PaCO2 52 mmHg and HCO3 24 mEq/L. This indicates:
en.e: Low pH with high PaCO2 means respiratory acidosis. Normal ranges: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45, HCO3 22–26.

en.q: A patient's monitor shows ventricular fibrillation and the patient is pulseless. The priority is:
o: Start CPR and defibrillate as soon as possible
en.e: Early defibrillation is the most important treatment for VF arrest.

en.q: A patient says, "I don't see the point of living anymore." The best response is:
o: "Don't talk like that. You have a lot to live for."
en.e: Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk. It opens communication and allows assessment and safety measures.

en.q: A patient taking lithium should be taught to:
o: Keep a normal, consistent salt and fluid intake and have blood levels checked
Stop the drug if they feel well
en.e: Low sodium or dehydration raises lithium levels and the risk of toxicity. Early toxicity includes vomiting, diarrhea and tremor.

en.q: A patient taking an MAO inhibitor should avoid:
o: Tyramine-rich foods such as aged cheese and cured meats
en.e: Tyramine can trigger a hypertensive crisis in patients taking MAOIs.

en.q: Alcohol withdrawal symptoms typically begin:
o: 6 to 24 hours after the last drink
1 to 2 weeks after the last drink
en.e: Delirium tremens usually appears around 48–72 hours. Benzodiazepines are commonly used.

en.q: Which is an example of therapeutic communication?
en.e: Open-ended questions encourage the patient to share. "Why" questions can sound judgmental.

en.q: A patient with schizophrenia says the television is sending him messages. The best response is:
o: "That must be frightening. I don't hear messages, but I'm here with you."
"What are the messages telling you to buy?"
en.e: Acknowledge the feelings, do not argue with or reinforce the delusion, and present reality calmly.

en.q: A patient taking clozapine needs regular monitoring of:
o: White blood cell and absolute neutrophil counts
en.e: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, a life-threatening fall in white blood cells.

en.q: High fever, severe muscle rigidity and altered consciousness in a patient taking an antipsychotic suggests:
en.e: Stop the antipsychotic, cool the patient and provide urgent medical care.

en.q: The first step when approaching an unresponsive adult in a hospital corridor is to:
o: Check that the scene is safe, then check responsiveness and call for help
Move the patient to a bed
en.e: Scene safety, responsiveness, call for help/AED, then check breathing and pulse, and start CPR if needed.

en.q: While setting up a sterile field for a dressing change, which action breaks sterile technique?
o: Keeping sterile gloved hands above waist level
Treating the outer 2.5 cm (1 inch) border of the field as unsterile
Opening the first flap of a sterile package away from the body
Reaching across the sterile field to pick up an item
en.e: Reaching over the field can drop contaminants onto it. Items below the waist or out of sight, and the outer border of the field, are considered unsterile.

en.q: When removing PPE after caring for a patient on airborne precautions, which item is removed last, after leaving the room?
en.e: Gloves, goggles and gown are removed first. The respirator is removed outside the room after the door is closed, followed by hand hygiene.

en.q: A patient has an MRSA wound infection. Which practice is correct?
o: Wear a gown and gloves on entering the room and use dedicated equipment such as a stethoscope
Wear an N95 respirator for all care
Use standard precautions only and share equipment between patients
Place the patient in a negative-pressure room
en.e: MRSA spreads by contact. Contact precautions and patient-dedicated equipment prevent transfer to other patients.

en.q: A nurse sustains a needlestick injury from a needle used on a patient. What should the nurse do first?
o: Squeeze the site hard and soak it in bleach
Finish the shift and report it if symptoms develop
Apply a bandage and wait for the patient's test results before reporting
Wash the site with soap and water and report the injury immediately
en.e: Wash with soap and water without scrubbing or caustic agents, then report at once so post-exposure assessment and prophylaxis can start promptly if needed.

en.q: When receiving a telephone order from a physician, the nurse should:
o: Write the order down and read it back to the prescriber to confirm it
Remember the order and write it down at the end of the shift
Ask a colleague to listen and write it later
Accept it only if the medication is already on the ward
en.e: "Write down and read back" reduces errors from mishearing. The order is then signed by the prescriber per policy.

en.q: Which way of writing a dose is safe and recommended?
en.e: Always use a leading zero and never a trailing zero; ".5" can be misread as 5 and "5.0" as 50. Write "units" in full because "U" can be misread as 0 or 4.

en.q: A nurse realizes that a patient was given the wrong medication. What is the nurse's first action?
o: Document the error in the nursing notes
Assess the patient for any effects of the medication
en.e: Patient safety comes first: assess and monitor the patient, then notify the prescriber, document and complete the incident report.

en.q: Which statement about incident (occurrence) reports is correct?
o: A copy is placed in the patient's medical record
The nurse writes "incident report completed" in the nursing notes
They are used to discipline the staff involved
The facts of the event are documented in the record, but the incident report itself is not mentioned there
en.e: Incident reports are quality-improvement tools. The medical record contains an objective account of what happened and the care given, not a reference to the report.

en.q: The nurse makes an error while writing a note in a paper record. The correct way to fix it is to:
o: Use correction fluid and rewrite the entry
Tear out the page and rewrite the note
Draw a single line through it, write "error" (or per policy), and add initials, date and time
en.e: The original entry must remain readable. Records must never be erased, obliterated or removed.

en.q: A caller says she is the patient's sister and asks how the patient's surgery went. The nurse should:
o: Check whether the patient has authorized sharing information with this person before giving any details
Give a full update because she is family
Read the operation notes to her
Tell her the diagnosis but not the medications
en.e: Patient information is confidential. It is shared only with people the patient has authorized, after confirming identity per hospital policy.

en.q: A patient is getting out of bed for the first time after surgery. To prevent orthostatic hypotension, the nurse should first:
o: Have the patient sit on the edge of the bed (dangle) for a few minutes before standing
Help the patient stand up quickly to save energy
Give an extra dose of analgesic
Keep the patient flat for 30 minutes before rising
en.e: Changing position gradually lets blood pressure adjust. Ask about dizziness and stay with the patient during the first walk.

en.q: Which technique reflects safe body mechanics when lifting?
o: Bending at the waist with straight knees
Holding the load at arm's length
Keeping a wide base of support, bending the knees and holding the load close to the body
en.e: A wide base, bent knees and the load close to the body's center of gravity reduce back strain. Use lifting devices and get help for heavy patients.

en.q: In which position should an adult be placed to receive a cleansing enema?
o: Left side-lying (Sims') with the right knee flexed
Right side-lying with both legs straight
en.e: The left lateral position follows the natural anatomy of the rectum and sigmoid colon, so the solution flows in more easily.

en.q: What is the most accurate method to confirm the initial placement of a blindly inserted nasogastric feeding tube before it is first used?
o: Listening over the stomach while injecting air
Placing the end of the tube in a cup of water
Asking whether the patient can talk
en.e: X-ray confirmation is the standard before the first feed or medication. Auscultation of injected air is unreliable. Aspirate pH and the external tube length are used for later checks.

en.q: To reduce the risk of aspiration during continuous enteral tube feeding, the nurse should keep the head of the bed:
en.e: Elevating the head of the bed reduces reflux and aspiration. Keep it raised unless contraindicated.

en.q: Which action helps prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection?
o: Keeping the drainage bag below the level of the bladder and off the floor
Disconnecting the catheter from the bag to empty it
Raising the bag above the patient during transfers
en.e: A closed system with downward flow prevents backflow of urine. Remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.

en.q: How should the nurse collect a urine specimen for culture from a patient with an indwelling catheter?
o: Pour urine from the drainage bag into the container
Disconnect the catheter from the tubing and drain the urine
Clean the sampling port and aspirate urine with a sterile syringe
Remove the catheter and send the tip
en.e: Urine in the bag has been standing and is not suitable for culture. Using the sampling port keeps the system closed.

en.q: Which intramuscular injection site is generally preferred for adults because it is away from major nerves and blood vessels?
en.e: The ventrogluteal site has thick muscle and avoids the sciatic nerve. The deltoid only takes small volumes (usually up to about 1 mL).

en.q: The Z-track technique for intramuscular injection is used to:
o: Prevent irritating medication from leaking back into the subcutaneous tissue
Make the injection less painful by giving it faster
Allow the needle to be reused
Avoid the need to clean the skin
en.e: Pulling the skin sideways before injecting seals the drug in the muscle once the skin is released, which reduces tissue staining and irritation.

en.q: What is the most reliable indicator of a patient's pain?
o: The nurse's observation of facial expression
The patient's own report of pain
en.e: Pain is what the patient says it is. Behavioral tools are used only for patients who cannot self-report.

en.q: To measure a pulse deficit, the nurse should:
o: Count the radial pulse twice and subtract the results
Have two nurses count the apical and radial pulses at the same time for one full minute
Compare the pulse with the respiratory rate
Compare the left and right radial pulses
en.e: The pulse deficit is the apical rate minus the radial rate. A deficit suggests that some heartbeats are not perfusing the periphery, as in atrial fibrillation.

en.q: Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small for the patient's arm will most likely give a reading that is:
en.e: A narrow cuff needs extra pressure to compress the artery. A cuff that is too large tends to give a falsely low reading.

en.q: Which IV solution can be given through the same line as a red blood cell transfusion?
o: Any solution that is already running
en.e: Dextrose can cause red cells to clump and hemolyze, and calcium in Lactated Ringer's can cause clotting. Only normal saline is compatible.

en.q: Using Maslow's hierarchy, which patient problem should the nurse address first?
o: Anxiety about a change in body image
Lack of knowledge about a new diet
Impaired swallowing with risk of aspiration
en.e: Physiological needs, especially airway, come before safety, belonging and esteem needs. Risk of aspiration threatens the airway.

en.q: A nurse writes: "The patient will walk 50 m with a walker by day 3 after surgery." Which step of the nursing process is this?
en.e: Setting measurable, time-limited goals is part of planning. Evaluation later checks whether the goal was met.

en.q: A patient speaks very little English and must give consent for a procedure. The nurse should:
o: Ask the patient's 12-year-old son to translate
Use simple gestures and have the patient sign
Ask a cleaner who speaks the same language
en.e: Trained interpreters give accurate, confidential translation. Family members, especially children, may omit or change information.

en.q: Which statement about physical restraints is correct?
o: A restraint order must be time-limited and cannot be written as PRN
A restraint order may be written "as needed" (PRN)
Restraints can be applied for staff convenience on busy shifts
Restrained patients need checks only once per shift
en.e: Restraints are a last resort after less restrictive measures fail. They need a current, time-limited order and frequent monitoring.

en.q: A wound bed has moist, beefy red, granular tissue. The nurse recognizes this as:
en.e: Granulation tissue is a sign of healing. Yellow slough or black eschar indicates devitalized tissue.

en.q: A patient is receiving home oxygen therapy. Which teaching point is most important for safety?
o: Oxygen can be increased whenever the patient feels tired
No smoking or open flames near the oxygen, because oxygen supports combustion
Cylinders should be stored lying in direct sunlight
Petroleum jelly is the best lubricant for the nostrils
en.e: Oxygen makes fires start easily and burn intensely. Use water-based lubricants and secure cylinders away from heat.

en.q: Which method best confirms that a patient has understood discharge teaching?
o: Giving the patient a printed leaflet
Asking the patient to explain or demonstrate the instructions in their own words (teach-back)
Having the patient sign the discharge form
en.e: Teach-back reveals gaps in understanding so the nurse can re-teach. A "yes" to "Do you understand?" is not reliable.

en.q: Fifteen minutes into a blood transfusion, the patient develops chills, fever and back pain. What should the nurse do first?
o: Stop the transfusion and keep the IV line open with 0.9% sodium chloride through new tubing
Slow the transfusion and recheck vital signs in 1 hour
Give paracetamol and continue the transfusion
en.e: Stop the blood at once to limit a possible hemolytic reaction, keep venous access, then notify the provider and blood bank and return the bag and tubing per policy.

en.q: A patient coughs on the second day after abdominal surgery and says, "Something gave way." The nurse sees loops of bowel protruding from the incision. What is the priority action?
o: Gently push the bowel back into the abdomen
Cover the wound with dry gauze and give oral fluids
Help the patient walk to reduce abdominal pressure
Cover the wound with sterile dressings moistened with sterile normal saline and notify the surgeon
en.e: Evisceration is a surgical emergency. Moist sterile dressings protect the organs; position the patient with knees flexed, keep NPO and monitor for shock.

en.q: Which group of findings is most consistent with hypothyroidism?
o: Cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation and bradycardia
Heat intolerance, weight loss and tachycardia
en.e: A low thyroid hormone level slows metabolism. Heat intolerance, tachycardia and exophthalmos suggest hyperthyroidism.

en.q: A patient with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is expected to have:
o: Low serum sodium and concentrated urine
High serum sodium and dilute urine
en.e: Excess ADH causes water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. Treatment usually includes fluid restriction and treating the cause.

en.q: After pituitary surgery, a patient passes large volumes of very dilute urine and is very thirsty. The nurse suspects diabetes insipidus. Which finding supports this?
en.e: Lack of ADH causes large volumes of dilute urine and a rising serum sodium. Monitor intake, output, weight and electrolytes.

en.q: A patient with type 1 diabetes has gastroenteritis and cannot eat much. What is the correct sick-day advice?
o: Halve fluid intake to prevent vomiting
Continue insulin, check blood glucose (and ketones) more often and keep drinking fluids
Check glucose only once a day
en.e: Illness raises glucose and the risk of DKA even when eating less. Stopping insulin is dangerous in type 1 diabetes.

en.q: Which foot-care instruction is correct for a patient with diabetes?
o: Soak the feet in hot water daily
Cut corns with a razor blade
Walk barefoot at home to toughen the skin
Inspect the feet daily, including between the toes, and always wear well-fitting footwear
en.e: Neuropathy reduces sensation, so injuries can go unnoticed. Daily inspection and protective footwear prevent ulcers and amputations.

en.q: A patient arrives at the emergency department with chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome. Within what time should a 12-lead ECG be obtained?
en.e: A 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival allows rapid identification of ST-elevation MI and timely reperfusion.

en.q: After a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery, which nursing action is correct?
o: Keep the affected leg straight and check the puncture site and distal pulses frequently
Help the patient walk within 15 minutes
Keep the hip flexed at 90 degrees
Check the pulses only in the unaffected leg
en.e: Keeping the leg straight for the prescribed time reduces bleeding. Watch for bleeding, hematoma, and changes in pulses, color or temperature of the leg.

en.q: A nurse is teaching a patient with heart failure. Which instruction is most important for detecting fluid retention early?
o: Check blood pressure once a month
Weigh yourself every morning at the same time, on the same scale, and report a rapid gain
Increase fluid intake when the ankles swell
Weigh yourself only when you feel short of breath
en.e: Daily weight is the most sensitive sign of fluid gain; about 1 kg equals 1 L of retained fluid.

en.q: A patient reports cramping calf pain when walking that goes away after a few minutes of rest. This is called:
en.e: Claudication results from arterial insufficiency. Other signs of peripheral arterial disease include weak pulses, cool pale skin and hair loss on the legs.

en.q: Which patient should the nurse see first?
o: A patient with diabetes whose pre-lunch glucose is 180 mg/dL (10 mmol/L)
A patient 3 hours after thyroidectomy who has new noisy, high-pitched breathing
A patient with COPD whose SpO2 is 90% on 2 L/min oxygen
A patient with heart failure who is asking for a bed bath
en.e: New stridor after neck surgery suggests airway obstruction from swelling, bleeding or nerve injury, an airway emergency. An SpO2 of 90% is within the usual COPD target.

en.q: During a severe asthma attack, the patient's wheezing stops and breath sounds become very faint. The nurse recognizes this as:
o: A sign the attack is resolving
Normal fatigue that needs no action
A sign of worsening obstruction and possible respiratory failure
en.e: A "silent chest" means very little air is moving. Call for urgent help and prepare for airway support.

en.q: A patient with suspected bacterial pneumonia has a new antibiotic order. When should the sputum specimen for culture be collected?
o: Before the first dose of antibiotic
Only if the patient does not improve
At the end of the antibiotic course
en.e: Antibiotics can kill organisms in the sample and give a false-negative culture. Do not delay antibiotics significantly while waiting for the sample.

en.q: When suctioning a tracheostomy, each suction pass should last no longer than:
en.e: Longer suctioning can cause hypoxemia, bradycardia and mucosal damage. Pre-oxygenate and apply suction only while withdrawing the catheter.

en.q: A patient's chest tube becomes disconnected from the drainage system. What should the nurse do immediately?
o: Clamp the tube for several hours
Place the end of the chest tube 2–3 cm under sterile water or saline
Leave it open to air and call the physician
en.e: Submerging the end restores a water seal while a new system is prepared. Prolonged clamping can cause a tension pneumothorax.

en.q: A patient with suspected appendicitis suddenly reports that the severe pain has gone away, and becomes febrile with a rigid abdomen. The nurse should suspect:
o: Perforation of the appendix with peritonitis
en.e: Sudden relief of pain can mean the appendix has ruptured. A rigid abdomen and fever suggest peritonitis, which needs urgent surgery.

en.q: Which presentation is typical of acute cholecystitis?
o: Right upper quadrant pain after a fatty meal that may radiate to the right shoulder
Left lower quadrant pain with diarrhea
Burning pain in the chest relieved by antacids
en.e: Gallbladder contraction after fatty food causes pain. Murphy's sign (pain stopping inspiration during right upper quadrant palpation) is often present.

en.q: Which laboratory result best supports a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
en.e: Lipase rises in acute pancreatitis and is more specific than amylase. Care includes NPO, IV fluids and pain control.

en.q: Before an abdominal paracentesis, the nurse should ask the patient to:
en.e: An empty bladder reduces the risk of puncturing it. Record weight and abdominal girth before and after the procedure.

en.q: Which type of viral hepatitis is spread mainly by the fecal-oral route?
en.e: Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated food and water; good hand hygiene and vaccination prevent it. Hepatitis B, C and D are bloodborne.

en.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease who is not yet on dialysis should be taught to:
o: Use salt substitutes instead of salt
Limit sodium and foods high in potassium and phosphorus
Drink as much fluid as possible
en.e: Failing kidneys cannot excrete potassium, phosphorus, sodium and fluid well. Most salt substitutes contain potassium.

en.q: A patient on peritoneal dialysis has cloudy dialysate drainage and abdominal pain. The nurse should suspect:
en.e: Cloudy effluent is often the first sign of peritonitis. Send a sample for cell count and culture and notify the provider.

en.q: After a total hip replacement through a posterior approach, the patient should be taught to avoid:
o: Sitting on a raised toilet seat
Keeping a pillow between the legs
Crossing the legs and bending the hip more than 90 degrees
en.e: Flexion beyond 90 degrees, adduction past the midline and internal rotation can dislocate the new hip.

en.q: A patient with a new forearm cast has severe pain that is not relieved by opioids and gets worse when the fingers are passively stretched. The nurse should suspect:
en.e: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs. Notify the provider urgently; loss of pulse is a late sign.

en.q: A patient has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in bed. What should the nurse do?
o: Put a tongue depressor between the teeth
Hold the arms and legs down firmly
Turn the patient to the side, protect the head, and time the seizure
en.e: Never put anything in the mouth or restrain movements. Side-lying keeps the airway clear; a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more needs emergency treatment.

en.q: A patient with a spinal cord injury at T4 suddenly has a severe headache, flushing above the injury and a blood pressure of 200/110 mmHg. What is the nurse's first action?
o: Recheck the blood pressure in 1 hour
en.e: This is autonomic dysreflexia. Sitting up lowers blood pressure; then find and remove the trigger, most often a full bladder or bowel.

en.q: A patient admitted with an acute stroke asks for a drink of water. What should the nurse do first?
o: Give small sips through a straw
Give the drink with the patient lying flat
Complete a swallow screen before giving anything by mouth
en.e: Dysphagia is common after stroke and can cause aspiration pneumonia. Keep the patient NPO, including oral medicines, until swallowing is screened.

en.q: On the day after a colostomy, the stoma appears dark purple-black. The nurse should:
o: Record it as a normal finding
Wait for it to turn pink in a few days
en.e: A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red. A dusky or black stoma suggests poor blood supply and necrosis.

en.q: After a mastectomy with axillary lymph node removal, which instruction is correct?
o: Avoid blood pressure measurements and injections on the affected arm
Avoid moving the affected arm for 3 months
Carry heavy shopping bags on the affected side
Wear tight jewelry on the affected arm
en.e: Removing lymph nodes raises the risk of lymphedema and infection in that arm. Gradual exercises as prescribed help recovery.

en.q: A patient is prescribed insulin lispro (a rapid-acting insulin) before meals. When should the nurse give it?
o: Within about 15 minutes before the meal, with food available
Only if the blood glucose is above 300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L)
en.e: Rapid-acting insulin starts working in about 15 minutes. Giving it without food ready can cause hypoglycemia.

en.q: When drawing up regular insulin and NPH insulin in the same syringe, the nurse should:
o: Draw up the regular (clear) insulin first
Draw up the NPH (cloudy) insulin first
en.e: "Clear before cloudy" prevents NPH from contaminating the regular insulin vial. NPH is gently rolled, not shaken.

en.q: A rare but serious adverse effect of metformin is:
en.e: The risk is higher with kidney impairment, dehydration or iodinated contrast. GI upset is the most common side effect.

en.q: How should a patient take levothyroxine?
o: On an empty stomach in the morning, 30–60 minutes before breakfast
en.e: Food, calcium and iron reduce absorption. Treatment is usually lifelong, and too much causes signs of hyperthyroidism.

en.q: A patient takes sublingual nitroglycerin for angina. Which drug must the patient avoid within the previous 24–48 hours?
en.e: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors combined with nitrates can cause severe, life-threatening hypotension.

en.q: When injecting enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe, the nurse should:
o: Expel the air bubble and inject into the deltoid
Leave the air bubble, inject into the abdomen at least 5 cm from the umbilicus, and not rub the site
Massage the site well after injection
en.e: Rubbing increases bruising. The prefilled syringe's air bubble is not expelled, so the full dose is delivered.

en.q: A patient has taken prednisolone daily for several months. Why must the drug not be stopped suddenly?
o: Abrupt withdrawal can cause acute adrenal insufficiency
en.e: Long-term steroids suppress the body's own cortisol production. The dose is tapered gradually.

en.q: A patient taking phenytoin long term should be taught to:
o: Drink alcohol to reduce side effects
Practice good oral hygiene and visit the dentist regularly
en.e: Gingival hyperplasia is a common side effect. Phenytoin has a narrow therapeutic range (about 10–20 mcg/mL), so levels are monitored.

en.q: A patient starting rifampin for tuberculosis should be told that:
o: Urine, sweat and tears may turn orange-red
The drug turns the skin blue
The drug can be stopped when the cough improves
en.e: The discoloration is harmless but may stain soft contact lenses. Liver function is monitored during treatment.

en.q: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is often given with isoniazid to prevent:
en.e: Isoniazid interferes with vitamin B6 metabolism. Isoniazid can also cause hepatotoxicity, so avoid alcohol and report jaundice.

en.q: Which adverse effect of long-term opioid therapy usually does NOT lessen as tolerance develops?
en.e: Tolerance develops to most opioid effects but not to constipation. A preventive bowel regimen should be started with regular opioids.

en.q: A patient taking atorvastatin should be told to report:
o: A mild headache on the first day
Unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness
en.e: Statins can cause myopathy and, rarely, rhabdomyolysis. Liver function may also be monitored.

en.q: For a patient receiving IV gentamicin, when should the blood sample for a trough level be drawn?
o: Just before the next dose is due
At any convenient time of day
en.e: The trough is the lowest drug level, just before the next dose. It helps ensure effective, non-toxic dosing.

en.q: Which instruction is correct for a patient taking oral iron tablets?
o: Take them with orange juice, and expect dark green or black stools
Take them with milk or antacids to protect the stomach
Stop them if stools become dark
Take them with tea to improve absorption
en.e: Vitamin C improves absorption, whereas milk, antacids and tea reduce it. Liquid iron should be taken through a straw to avoid staining teeth.

en.q: Which effects are expected after a dose of atropine?
o: Tachycardia, dry mouth and urinary retention
en.e: Atropine blocks the parasympathetic nervous system ("can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't poop").

en.q: A patient using inhaled salbutamol frequently reports shakiness and a fast heartbeat. The nurse recognizes these as:
o: Common side effects of a beta-2 agonist
Signs of hypoglycemia caused by the drug
en.e: Salbutamol can cause tremor, tachycardia and nervousness. Increasing need for the reliever suggests poorly controlled asthma.

en.q: After using an inhaled corticosteroid such as budesonide, the patient should:
o: Use it only during acute attacks
Rinse the mouth with water and spit it out
en.e: Rinsing reduces the risk of oral candidiasis and hoarseness. Inhaled steroids are controllers, not rescue medications.

en.q: Which medication is considered a high-alert medication that requires extra safeguards such as an independent double check?
en.e: High-alert medications (such as insulin, heparin, opioids and concentrated electrolytes) can cause serious harm if given in error.

en.q: Digoxin 0.25 mg orally is prescribed. The tablets available are 125 micrograms (mcg) each. How many tablets should the nurse give?
en.e: 0.25 mg = 250 mcg. 250 mcg ÷ 125 mcg per tablet = 2 tablets. Convert to the same unit before calculating.

en.q: Morphine 4 mg IV is prescribed. The vial contains 10 mg/mL. How many mL should the nurse draw up?
en.e: Dose ÷ concentration: 4 mg ÷ 10 mg/mL = 0.4 mL. 2.5 mL results from dividing the wrong way round.

en.q: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours is prescribed for a patient who weighs 154 lb. Use 1 kg = 2.2 lb. What is each dose?
en.e: 154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg; 70 kg × 1 mg/kg = 70 mg per dose. 140 mg is the total daily amount, not a single dose.

en.q: 1,000 mL of IV fluid is to infuse over 6 hours through a set with a drop factor of 15 drops/mL. What is the rate in drops per minute? (Round to the nearest whole drop.)
en.e: (1,000 mL × 15 drops/mL) ÷ 360 min = 41.7, about 42 drops/min. 167 is the rate in mL/h, not drops/min.

en.q: An infusion is to run at 50 mL/h through a microdrip set (60 drops/mL). How many drops per minute should the nurse set?
en.e: (50 mL × 60 drops/mL) ÷ 60 min = 50 drops/min. With a 60 drops/mL set, drops/min always equals mL/h.

en.q: An IV antibiotic in 100 mL is to be infused over 30 minutes using a pump. At what rate (mL/h) should the pump be set?
en.e: Pumps are set in mL per hour: 100 mL ÷ 0.5 h = 200 mL/h.

en.q: A heparin infusion of 25,000 units in 250 mL is running at 12 mL/h. How many units per hour is the patient receiving?
en.e: Concentration = 25,000 ÷ 250 = 100 units/mL; 100 units/mL × 12 mL/h = 1,200 units/h.

en.q: A patient weighing 80 kg is to start a heparin infusion at 18 units/kg/h. The bag contains 25,000 units in 500 mL. At what rate (mL/h) should the pump be set? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
en.e: 18 × 80 = 1,440 units/h. Concentration = 25,000 ÷ 500 = 50 units/mL. 1,440 ÷ 50 = 28.8, about 29 mL/h.

en.q: Dopamine is prescribed at 5 mcg/kg/min for a 70 kg patient. The bag contains 400 mg in 250 mL. What pump rate (mL/h) is needed? (Round to one decimal place.)
en.e: Concentration = 400,000 mcg ÷ 250 mL = 1,600 mcg/mL. Dose = 5 × 70 × 60 = 21,000 mcg/h. 21,000 ÷ 1,600 = 13.1 mL/h. Forgetting to multiply by 60 minutes gives 0.2.

en.q: After reconstitution, a vial contains 1 g of antibiotic in 4 mL. The order is 750 mg. How many mL should the nurse give?
en.e: 1 g = 1,000 mg, so the concentration is 250 mg/mL. 750 mg ÷ 250 mg/mL = 3 mL.

en.q: A child weighing 12 kg is prescribed 250 mg of a drug every 8 hours. The safe range is 25–50 mg/kg/day in divided doses. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the dose because it is within the safe range
Give the dose because each single dose is below 600 mg
Give the dose and document that it is low
Hold the dose and contact the prescriber because the daily dose exceeds the safe maximum
en.e: Safe range: 12 × 25 = 300 mg/day to 12 × 50 = 600 mg/day. Ordered: 250 mg × 3 = 750 mg/day, which is above the maximum.

en.q: A regular insulin infusion contains 100 units in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride. The order is 6 units/h. At what rate should the pump be set?
en.e: Concentration = 100 units ÷ 100 mL = 1 unit/mL, so 6 units/h = 6 mL/h. Monitor blood glucose hourly or per protocol.

en.q: During the third stage of labor, which signs indicate that the placenta has separated?
o: The uterus becomes soft and boggy and the cord shortens
A gush of blood, lengthening of the umbilical cord, and the uterus becoming firm and globular
Strong urge to push and crowning
en.e: These signs usually appear within minutes after birth. Never pull hard on the cord before separation, as this can invert the uterus.

en.q: A woman at 32 weeks of gestation has sudden, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding. The nurse should suspect placenta previa and should avoid:
o: Placing the woman on her side
en.e: A vaginal exam can disrupt the placenta over the cervix and cause massive hemorrhage. Diagnosis is made by ultrasound.

en.q: A pregnant woman involved in a car accident has dark vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain and a rigid, board-like uterus. These findings suggest:
en.e: Abruption (premature separation of the placenta) is painful, and bleeding may be concealed. It threatens both mother and fetus.

en.q: After the membranes rupture, the nurse sees the umbilical cord at the vaginal opening. What should the nurse do?
o: Push the cord back into the vagina
Ask the woman to push hard to speed the birth
Call for help, relieve pressure on the cord with a gloved hand on the presenting part, and position the woman knee-chest or in Trendelenburg
Cover the cord with a dry towel and wait for the physician
en.e: Cord prolapse is an emergency. Lifting the presenting part off the cord restores fetal blood flow while urgent birth is arranged. If the cord is outside the vagina, keep it warm and moist and handle it as little as possible.

en.q: A woman receiving an oxytocin infusion has 6 contractions in 10 minutes (averaged over 30 minutes) and the fetal heart rate shows late decelerations. What is the nurse's first action?
o: Lay the woman flat on her back
en.e: This is tachysystole with fetal compromise. Stop oxytocin, reposition to the side, give IV fluids, and notify the provider.

en.q: A woman's last menstrual period began on 10 June. Using Naegele's rule, what is her estimated date of delivery?
en.e: Naegele's rule: first day of the LMP + 7 days − 3 months (+ 1 year). 10 June + 7 days = 17 June; − 3 months = 17 March.

en.q: A woman is pregnant now. She has one living child born at 39 weeks and had a miscarriage at 10 weeks. How is she described?
en.e: Gravida counts all pregnancies, including the current one (3). Para counts births at 20 weeks or more (1); the early miscarriage is not counted in para.

en.q: Screening for gestational diabetes with an oral glucose tolerance test is usually done at:
en.e: Insulin resistance rises in the second half of pregnancy. Women at high risk may be screened earlier.

en.q: At about 20 weeks of gestation, the fundal height is normally found at the level of the:
en.e: From about 20 to 36 weeks, fundal height in centimeters roughly equals the number of weeks of gestation.

en.q: A woman at 36 weeks of gestation feels dizzy and faint while lying flat on her back. What should the nurse do?
o: Raise her legs and keep her flat
Sit her upright and give oral fluids only
Give oxygen and keep her supine
Turn her onto her left side
en.e: The heavy uterus compresses the inferior vena cava, reducing venous return (supine hypotensive syndrome). A lateral position relieves it.

en.q: A woman who gave birth 4 hours ago has a firm fundus 2 cm above the umbilicus, deviated to the right. What should the nurse do first?
o: Record this as a normal finding
en.e: A full bladder pushes the uterus up and to the side and can prevent it from contracting well, increasing bleeding.

en.q: Which postpartum woman should the nurse see first?
o: A woman 2 days after birth with pinkish-brown lochia
A woman 6 hours after birth who has soaked a perineal pad in 15 minutes
A breastfeeding mother asking about sore nipples
A woman 1 day after birth with a firm fundus at the umbilicus
en.e: Saturating a pad in 15 minutes indicates excessive bleeding and possible postpartum hemorrhage. The other findings are expected or non-urgent.

en.q: Which finding in a woman 1 week after birth requires urgent intervention?
o: Crying easily and feeling tired for a few days
Mild anxiety about caring for the baby
Difficulty sleeping because of night feeds
Hearing voices telling her to harm her baby
en.e: Hallucinations suggest postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency with risk to mother and baby. Mild tearfulness in the first two weeks is common ("baby blues").

en.q: The normal respiratory rate of a healthy full-term newborn at rest is:
en.e: Newborn breathing is irregular, so count for a full minute. Persistent rates above 60, grunting or retractions suggest respiratory distress.

en.q: Immediately after birth, what is the best way to prevent heat loss in a healthy newborn?
o: Dry the baby thoroughly and place the baby skin-to-skin with the mother
Bathe the baby right away in warm water
Leave the baby uncovered under a fan
Weigh the baby on a cold scale first
en.e: Wet newborns lose heat quickly by evaporation. Drying, skin-to-skin contact and a hat reduce heat loss.

en.q: Erythromycin eye ointment is applied to newborns to prevent:
en.e: Infection acquired during vaginal birth can cause severe conjunctivitis and blindness. The ointment is given soon after birth.

en.q: A newborn of a mother with diabetes is jittery and feeding poorly 2 hours after birth. The nurse should first:
o: Give a bath to calm the baby
Wrap the baby tightly and recheck in 4 hours
en.e: Babies of diabetic mothers have high insulin levels after birth and are at risk of hypoglycemia. Jitteriness and poor feeding are typical signs.

en.q: A newborn is receiving phototherapy for jaundice. Which nursing action is correct?
o: Apply baby lotion to the skin
Keep the baby fully dressed under the lights
Cover the eyes with eye shields and monitor temperature and hydration
en.e: Shields protect the eyes, and maximal skin exposure makes treatment effective. Phototherapy increases fluid loss, so feeding continues.

en.q: To reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome, parents should place the baby to sleep:
o: On the side, propped with pillows
On the back, on a firm flat surface without loose bedding
In the parents' bed between them
en.e: Back-sleeping on a firm surface, with no pillows, bumpers or soft toys, is the main safe-sleep recommendation.

en.q: A healthy infant usually begins to smile socially at about:
en.e: The social smile appears around 6–8 weeks and is one of the earliest social milestones.

en.q: A 9-month-old has sudden episodes of severe abdominal pain with drawing up of the legs and passes "red currant jelly" stools. The nurse suspects:
en.e: One bowel segment telescopes into another. A sausage-shaped abdominal mass may be felt. It is an emergency.

en.q: A 4-week-old infant has projectile, non-bilious vomiting after feeds and seems hungry afterwards. An olive-shaped mass is felt in the upper abdomen. The likely diagnosis is:
en.e: Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle blocks gastric emptying. Watch for dehydration and metabolic alkalosis; treatment is surgical.

en.q: Failure of a full-term newborn to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life suggests:
en.e: Absent ganglion cells in part of the colon prevent peristalsis. Most healthy newborns pass meconium within 24–48 hours.

en.q: A child is admitted with a suspected Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma). Which nursing action is most important?
o: Encourage the child to play contact sports
Avoid palpating the abdomen and post a "do not palpate" sign
en.e: Palpation can rupture the encapsulated tumor and spread cancer cells.

en.q: A child with tetralogy of Fallot suddenly becomes very cyanotic and breathless while crying. What should the nurse do first?
o: Place the child in a knee-chest position
Encourage the child to keep crying
Give a large volume of oral fluid
en.e: Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance and sends more blood to the lungs. Oxygen and medication may follow.

en.q: Two weeks after a sore throat, a child has cola-colored urine, puffy eyes and high blood pressure. The nurse suspects:
en.e: An immune reaction after streptococcal infection damages the glomeruli, causing hematuria, edema and hypertension. Monitor BP, weight and urine output.

en.q: Which pain assessment tool is most suitable for a 4-year-old child who can talk?
en.e: Young children can point to a face that matches their pain. Numeric scales need number concepts usually present in older children; FLACC is for children who cannot self-report.

en.q: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally is prescribed for a child weighing 13 kg. The suspension is 120 mg/5 mL. How many mL should be given? (Round to one decimal place.)
en.e: Dose = 15 × 13 = 195 mg. Volume = 195 ÷ 120 × 5 = 8.125, about 8.1 mL. 1.6 mL results from forgetting to multiply by 5 mL.

en.q: An infant who is awake is choking and cannot cry or cough. Following basic life support guidelines, the nurse should give:
o: Abdominal thrusts until the object comes out
Blind finger sweeps of the mouth
Cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts
Two rescue breaths and then check the pulse
en.e: Abdominal thrusts are not used in infants because of the risk of liver injury. If the infant becomes unresponsive, start CPR.

en.q: To reduce the risk of neural tube defects, women planning a pregnancy are advised to take:
o: Iron 200 mg daily from the first trimester
Folic acid 0.4 mg (400 mcg) daily, starting before conception
Vitamin C only after the first scan
en.e: The neural tube closes in the first month, often before pregnancy is known. Higher doses are prescribed for women at high risk.

en.q: A conscious adult is choking, cannot speak or cough, and clutches the throat. What should the nurse do?
o: Encourage the patient to drink water
Give abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unresponsive
en.e: Abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) are used for severe airway obstruction in conscious adults. If the patient becomes unresponsive, start CPR.

en.q: An adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally but has a definite pulse. How often should the nurse give rescue breaths?
en.e: For respiratory arrest with a pulse, give 1 breath every 6 seconds and recheck the pulse about every 2 minutes. Start CPR if the pulse is lost.

en.q: Two rescuers are performing CPR on a child. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
en.e: For infants and children, 2-rescuer CPR uses 15:2; a single rescuer uses 30:2.

en.q: The cardiac monitor of a pulseless patient shows asystole. What is the correct management?
o: Continue high-quality CPR and give epinephrine as soon as possible
en.e: Asystole is not a shockable rhythm. Treat with CPR, epinephrine and a search for reversible causes (Hs and Ts).

en.q: During adult cardiac arrest, epinephrine is given at a dose of:
en.e: Each dose is followed by a saline flush. IM epinephrine (0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL) is the dose for anaphylaxis, not cardiac arrest.

en.q: For adult ventricular fibrillation that persists after defibrillation and epinephrine, the first dose of amiodarone is:
en.e: A second dose of 150 mg may be given. Lidocaine is an alternative.

en.q: A patient has a heart rate of 38/min, hypotension and dizziness. Which drug is the first choice for this symptomatic bradycardia?
en.e: If atropine is ineffective, transcutaneous pacing or an infusion of dopamine or epinephrine may be used.

en.q: A stable patient has supraventricular tachycardia that does not respond to vagal maneuvers. How should adenosine be given?
o: As a rapid IV push followed immediately by a saline flush
en.e: Adenosine has a half-life of only a few seconds, so it must reach the heart quickly. Warn the patient about brief chest discomfort or a pause on the monitor.

en.q: A patient with a tachycardia and a pulse is hypotensive, confused and has chest pain. What is the recommended treatment?
en.e: Unstable tachycardia with a pulse is treated with synchronized cardioversion. Synchronizing avoids delivering the shock during the T wave.

en.q: After chest trauma, a patient has severe dyspnea, absent breath sounds on the right, tracheal deviation to the left and falling blood pressure. The nurse suspects:
en.e: Trapped air pushes the mediastinum to the opposite side and reduces venous return. Immediate needle decompression or chest tube insertion is needed.

en.q: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins after a stab wound to the chest suggest:
en.e: This is Beck's triad. Blood in the pericardial sac prevents the heart from filling. Treatment is urgent pericardiocentesis or surgery.

en.q: After a head injury, clear fluid drains from the patient's nose. Which action is correct?
o: Do not insert anything into the nose and report the finding immediately
Ask the patient to blow the nose
en.e: The fluid may be cerebrospinal fluid from a skull base fracture. A "halo" ring on gauze suggests CSF. Nasal tubes and suctioning risk infection and brain injury.

en.q: A trauma patient with a suspected cervical spine injury is unresponsive. Which method should be used to open the airway?
o: Turning the head to one side
en.e: The jaw thrust opens the airway while limiting neck movement. Maintain spinal motion restriction.

en.q: A construction worker collapses outdoors in the summer heat. He is confused, his skin is hot, and his core temperature is 41°C. What is the priority?
o: Give oral fluids and wait 1 hour
Begin rapid cooling, such as cold-water immersion or ice packs with evaporative cooling
en.e: Heat stroke is an emergency with central nervous system dysfunction and core temperature above 40°C. Rapid cooling reduces death and organ damage; antipyretics do not work.

en.q: A farm worker has pinpoint pupils, heavy salivation, sweating, vomiting, diarrhea and wheezing after spraying pesticide. Which drug is the main antidote?
en.e: Organophosphates cause cholinergic excess. Atropine is given until secretions dry; staff must wear PPE and decontaminate the patient.

en.q: A patient rescued from a house fire has a headache and confusion, and the pulse oximeter reads 98%. The nurse suspects carbon monoxide poisoning. What is the priority treatment?
o: Room air, because the SpO2 is normal
en.e: Standard pulse oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, so SpO2 is falsely normal. High-flow oxygen speeds CO elimination.

en.q: In septic shock requiring vasopressors, the usual initial target mean arterial pressure (MAP) is:
en.e: A MAP of 65 mmHg or more maintains organ perfusion. Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor.

en.q: The low-pressure alarm sounds on a patient's mechanical ventilator. The most likely cause is:
o: Disconnection of the circuit or a cuff leak
en.e: Low pressure means air is escaping. High-pressure alarms are caused by secretions, coughing, biting or kinked tubing. If the cause cannot be found, ventilate manually with a bag-valve device.

en.q: Which measure helps prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia?
o: Elevating the head of the bed 30–45 degrees and providing regular oral care
Routinely changing the ventilator circuit every day
en.e: Head elevation reduces aspiration. Oral care, daily sedation review and early weaning are also part of prevention bundles.

en.q: A patient rescued from a fire in an enclosed room has singed nasal hairs, soot in the sputum and a hoarse voice. The nurse should anticipate:
o: Early intubation because of airway swelling
en.e: These are signs of inhalation injury. Airway edema can develop rapidly and make later intubation very difficult.

en.q: Using START mass-casualty triage, an adult who is breathing at 36 breaths per minute is tagged:
en.e: In START, a respiratory rate above 30 per minute places the patient in the immediate (red) category.

en.q: Which patient in the emergency department should the nurse assess first?
o: A young adult with a painful, swollen ankle after a fall
A 55-year-old with crushing chest pain and sweating
A child with a fever of 38.5°C who is playing and drinking
A patient with a forearm cut whose bleeding is controlled
en.e: Chest pain with sweating suggests acute coronary syndrome, a threat to life. The others are stable.

en.q: Before starting an insulin infusion for diabetic ketoacidosis, which laboratory value is most important to check?
en.e: Insulin moves potassium into cells and can cause dangerous hypokalemia. If potassium is low, it must be replaced before insulin is started.

en.q: A patient with severe depression suddenly appears calm and cheerful and gives away personal possessions. The nurse should:
o: Reduce observation because the patient is improving
Recognize these as possible warning signs of suicide and assess for a plan
en.e: A sudden lift in mood may mean the patient has decided on suicide. Ask directly about suicidal ideas and a plan and keep the patient safe.

en.q: A patient taking an SSRI is given tramadol and develops agitation, fever, sweating, tremor and muscle clonus. The nurse suspects:
en.e: Combining serotonergic drugs can cause serotonin syndrome. Clonus and hyperreflexia help distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

en.q: An agitated patient is shouting and pacing in the ward. Which action is best for de-escalation?
o: Stand close and raise your voice so you are heard
Turn your back to show you are not a threat
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and make sure you have a clear exit
Tell the patient that security will restrain him
en.e: Calm, simple communication and a safe environment reduce aggression. Keep the exit clear and call for help if needed.

en.q: A patient with severe anorexia nervosa starts nutritional rehabilitation. Which laboratory value is most important to monitor for refeeding syndrome?
en.e: Refeeding shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. Severe hypophosphatemia can cause heart failure and arrhythmias.

en.q: Which group of findings suggests opioid withdrawal?
o: Pinpoint pupils, drowsiness and slow breathing
Dilated pupils, yawning, runny nose and diarrhea
Hypothermia and slow heart rate only
en.e: Withdrawal is very uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening in adults. Pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression indicate opioid intoxication.

en.q: A patient who started haloperidol yesterday develops a sudden spasm of the neck muscles with the head twisted to one side. The nurse anticipates treatment with:
en.e: This is acute dystonia, an extrapyramidal side effect that often appears within days. Anticholinergic drugs relieve it quickly.

en.q: A patient's serum potassium is 7.0 mmol/L and the ECG shows wide QRS complexes. Which drug is given first to protect the heart?
en.e: Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes but does not lower potassium. Insulin with glucose and other treatments then shift or remove potassium.
